h1:
Ban Tha Wat
Indigo Village on Nong Han Lake
intro: If you want to see one of Sakon Nakhon's indigo-dyeing villages without driving far out of town, Ban Tha Wat in Lao Po Daeng sub-district, right on Nong Han lake, is the easy answer. It's only about a 15-minute drive from the city centre. Here a group of local women run the whole indigo process themselves — from fermenting the dye in the vat to dyeing and weaving the finished cloth — and they let you watch the real thing and buy fabric straight from the makers. What makes Tha Wat special is that it's an old community on the lake, where people dye indigo alongside fishing and curing fish, so you can see the indigo vats, take a raft out for a fish lunch, and buy cloth all in one trip.
chips: 🛶 Pair it with a Nong Han raft trip
🛍️ Buy cloth straight from the makers

blocks.html: Sakon Nakhon is Thailand's indigo-cloth province, with dyeing communities scattered across the whole area — from far-out model villages like Ban Don Koi to designer brands around the Phu Phan hills. But if you're short on time and want to see the real process without driving way out, Ban Tha Wat hits the sweet spot. It's the closest village to town, just 15 minutes away, and it has a lakeside setting on Nong Han that the other communities don't.

Ban Tha Wat is an old community on Nong Han lake, in Lao Po Daeng sub-district of Mueang district. The people here come from several ethnic groups mixed together — Thai Yo, Thai Kaleung, Phu Thai and So — and they've always lived with the water: fishing on Nong Han, curing it into pickled fish (pla som), fermented fish (pla ra) and sun-dried fish, and weaving indigo cloth for the household. Today the women's group has turned indigo into a craft and opened the village up as a place to come, watch, and buy on the spot.

blocks.text: Why Ban Tha Wat, when Sakon Nakhon has so many indigo villages

blocks.html: Sakon Nakhon has plenty of indigo communities to choose from, each with its own strengths. Ban Tha Wat wins on location and atmosphere — it's perfect if you want to see the real indigo process without planning a whole day around it.

items: Closest to town — about 12–15 km from Sakon Nakhon city, a 15-minute drive, easy to slot into a half-day trip.
On Nong Han lake — an old community on the largest lake in Isan, with wide-open water views the other indigo villages don't have.
See it all in one place — from the fermenting vat to the dyeing to the weaving loom, then buy cloth straight from the maker.
Easy to combine — take a raft out for a fish lunch on Nong Han, visit a temple, and see Dvaravati-era antiques at the lakeside temple, all in one trip.

blocks.text: Watch the indigo ferment — what it takes to make one vat of dye

blocks.html: The heart of indigo cloth is the vat. Indigo dyers like to say the dye is a living thing — you have to feed and tend it every day so it doesn't die. At Ban Tha Wat the women's group still does the whole thing from scratch, and if you time it right you'll see these steps for real and understand exactly why genuine indigo costs more than chemically dyed cloth.

items.name: Soaking the indigo leaves
items.blurb: Fresh indigo leaves are soaked in water for about 18–24 hours until the water changes colour, then lime is added and the mixture is beaten until it foams. The deep blue sediment that settles at the bottom is the indigo paste (pieak khram), the starting raw material for the dye.

items.name: Building the indigo vat
items.blurb: The indigo paste is mixed with ash water and lime in the vat, then stirred (jok) every day for about 7–10 days so the indigo slowly revives until the dye turns a yellowish-green. This step takes the most skill — if the vat doesn't come alive, the indigo won't take to the cloth.

items.name: Keeping the indigo alive
items.blurb: Dyers say indigo is a living colour — you keep it going in the vat like tending a sourdough starter, feeding and stirring it every day so it doesn't die. The longer a vat has been kept alive, the more even and beautiful its colour, and it becomes a point of pride for each household.
items.meta: Tend daily · older vats give steadier colour

items.name: Dyeing and airing to bring up the colour
items.blurb: Once the dye is ready, you dip the cloth or yarn into the vat, squeeze it through, then lift it out to air. Cloth just out of the vat is green, then slowly turns blue as it meets the oxygen — a reaction that's oddly satisfying to watch. You dip again and again to build up the depth of colour.
items.meta: Dip and air, repeated until the colour builds

blocks.title: Why genuine indigo costs more
blocks.html: Once you see that building the vat takes a week, the indigo has to be tended every day, the cloth is dyed over and over, and then it still has to be hand-woven, you understand why real indigo costs several times more than chemically dyed fabric. What you're paying for is the time and skill of the maker, not just the cloth.

blocks.text: Watch the weaving — from tying patterns to finished cloth

blocks.html: After dyeing, the indigo yarn goes onto the hand looms. Most of the weavers at Ban Tha Wat are local women and elders who've been doing this since their mothers' generation. The cloth ranges from plain pieces in shades of indigo, from light to dark, to mat-mi (ikat) cloth where the yarn is tie-dyed before weaving to create the pattern. A single piece takes anywhere from several days to a week depending on how intricate the pattern is. Stand and watch a while and you'll see this work really does take patience and a steady hand.

items: Plain indigo cloth — woven in shades of blue from light to dark, good for tailoring a shirt or for home decor.
Mat-mi (ikat) cloth — the yarn is tie-dyed before weaving; the finer the pattern, the longer it takes and the higher the price.
Small souvenir pieces — handkerchiefs, scarves and tote bags, easy on the wallet as gifts to take home.
Meet the actual weavers — ask about the origin and the patterns directly; the people who made it can tell you which vat it was dyed in and how many days it took to weave.

blocks.text: Try dyeing your own — a workshop for visitors

blocks.html: The community group lets visitors try indigo dyeing for themselves if you want to take home a keepsake. Most people dye a handkerchief, a scarf or a tote bag, and watch the colour shift from green to blue with their own eyes. It's a fun activity to do with kids or as a group.

items: What you'll do — tie the cloth in whatever pattern you like, dip and dye it in the indigo yourself, then air it to bring up the colour — and go home with a one-of-a-kind piece.
How long it takes — about 1–2 hours per piece, depending on the pattern and how many times you dip it.
Rough price — a workshop dyeing a small piece runs about 150–350 THB per piece, usually including the cloth.
Book ahead — the community group runs this as a household craft, not a workshop that's open all the time, so messaging their page or calling to book 1–2 days ahead is the safer bet.

blocks.title: Leave time for the colour to set
blocks.html: Freshly dyed cloth needs to air-dry and set before you can take it home without it smudging, so leave a bit of buffer time at the end, and bag it separately for the trip home to keep the colour off everything else in your bag.

blocks.text: How to buy genuine indigo cloth

blocks.html: The upside of buying at Ban Tha Wat is that you buy straight from the maker — you can ask which vat it was dyed in and how many dips it took, and you usually get a better price than souvenir shops in town or roadside stalls on the highway. The market has both genuine indigo and chemically dyed imitations, which can differ in price by several times. Here's how to tell them apart.

items: Smell — genuine indigo has a faint natural indigo scent, not the sharp chemical smell of synthetic dye.
Colour — real indigo is a deep, slightly muted blue with depth and not perfectly even; chemical dye looks too bright and too uniformly flat.
Colour bleed — genuine indigo bleeds a little in the first few washes, which is normal for a natural dye, not a defect.
The fabric — hand-woven indigo cotton feels cool and breathes well to wear, unlike factory cloth.
Ask the origin — buying from the maker, you can ask straight out whether they dyed it themselves and how many days the vat took; the real makers can answer all of it.

blocks.title: Rough prices to compare against
blocks.html: An indigo handkerchief or small piece starts around 80–150 THB. An indigo scarf runs about 250–500 THB depending on the fabric and pattern. An indigo-dyed shirt is around 500–1,500 THB depending on the cut. A hand-woven mat-mi piece with a fine pattern can run from a thousand to several thousand THB each. Buying straight from the community is usually cheaper than shops in town or along the highway.

blocks.text: Make the most of Ban Tha Wat — indigo plus Nong Han

blocks.html: What gives Ban Tha Wat its charm — and what the other indigo villages don't have — is Nong Han, the largest freshwater lake in Isan, right in front of the village. People here dye indigo alongside fishing and curing fish, so you can build a trip that sees the indigo, takes a raft out for a fish lunch, and visits a temple, all in one unhurried day.

blocks.label: Morning half-day
blocks.title: See the indigo, dye your own, buy cloth

items.activity: Drive out from Sakon Nakhon to Ban Tha Wat and visit the indigo weaving group — see the fermenting vat, the dyeing, and the weaving loom.
items.note: About a 15-minute drive; book ahead if you want to catch the dyeing live.

items.activity: Try dyeing your own handkerchief or scarf, then pick out indigo cloth straight from the makers.
items.note: The workshop takes about 1–2 hours; leave time for the colour to set.

blocks.label: Afternoon half-day
blocks.title: Raft fish lunch and a lakeside temple

items.activity: Head out on a raft on Nong Han and order fresh fish from the community — grilled, fried, or in tom yum — and eat on the raft with the wide lake view.
items.note: Several raft operators to choose from; weekends get busy, so go early.

items.activity: Stop at the temple to pay respects and see the carved boundary stones (bai sema) and Dvaravati-era antiques at the lakeside temple in the community.
items.note: Ban Tha Wat has an old lakeside temple that keeps these antiquities.

items.activity: Pick up some of the community's cured fish — pla som, pla ra and sun-dried fish — to take home, then head back into town.
items.note: Cured fish is Tha Wat's signature take-home gift.

blocks.text: Getting there and the best time to go

items: Location — Ban Tha Wat, Lao Po Daeng sub-district, Mueang Sakon Nakhon, on Nong Han lake, about 12–15 km from the city.
Driving — about a 15-minute drive from the Sakon Nakhon city area; having your own car is by far the easiest, as public transport barely reaches here.
Best time — come from morning to late morning for the atmosphere and gentler sun; weekdays are quieter and easier for chatting with the makers.
Rafting — the Nong Han rafts are busiest in the hot season and on holidays; on weekends go early to book a raft.

blocks.title: An honest heads-up
blocks.html: Ban Tha Wat is a community where people actually live, not a village staged for tourism. On some unannounced visits you might not catch anyone dyeing right then, or the indigo vat might not be alive yet. If you're set on seeing the full process or want to learn to dye, contact the group ahead of time. If you just want to buy cloth or take a raft out for a fish lunch, you can drop in whenever.

faq.q: Is Ban Tha Wat far from Sakon Nakhon town?
faq.a: Not far. It's in Lao Po Daeng sub-district, Mueang district, on Nong Han lake, about 12–15 km from Sakon Nakhon city — roughly a 15-minute drive. It's the closest indigo-dyeing village to town, perfect to slot into a half-day trip.

faq.q: Can you actually watch the indigo fermenting and weaving at Ban Tha Wat?
faq.a: Yes. The women's group here still does the whole thing themselves — from fermenting the indigo in the vat to dyeing and weaving the finished cloth — and they let you come in to watch and ask questions. If you want to see the full process or try dyeing yourself, contact the group to book 1–2 days ahead, as this is a household craft and isn't set up for demos at all hours.

faq.q: How much does it cost to try indigo dyeing at Ban Tha Wat?
faq.a: A workshop dyeing a small piece like a handkerchief or scarf runs about 150–350 THB per piece, usually with the cloth included, and takes around 1–2 hours, leaving you with a one-of-a-kind piece to take home. Booking the group ahead is a good idea, especially for a larger group.

faq.q: How much does Ban Tha Wat indigo cloth cost, and how do you spot the real thing?
faq.a: A handkerchief or small piece starts around 80–150 THB, a scarf about 250–500 THB, a shirt about 500–1,500 THB, and a hand-woven mat-mi piece with a fine pattern from a thousand THB up. Real indigo has a faint indigo scent, a deep slightly muted blue that isn't perfectly even, and a little colour bleed in the first washes, which is normal. Buying from the maker, you can ask about its origin and usually get a better price than souvenir shops.

faq.q: Besides seeing the indigo, what else can you do at Ban Tha Wat?
faq.a: Ban Tha Wat sits on Nong Han, the largest freshwater lake in Isan, so you can take a raft out for a fresh community fish lunch — grilled, fried, or in tom yum — pay respects at the temple and see the carved boundary stones and Dvaravati-era antiques at the lakeside temple, and pick up the community's cured fish (pla som, pla ra, sun-dried fish) as gifts. You can fit the indigo, the raft and the temple into one day.
